m00.body:
## What this pack is steering

The rep's words are "veterinary practices in Orkney", direct motion, GB, email only, 10 names wanted in 3 weeks. Two things about that brief have to be said before a single search is run, because they shape everything the campaign agent can legitimately do with this pack.

**First, the geography is extremely small.** Orkney is a Scottish island council area with a resident population in the low tens of thousands. The number of veterinary premises registered there is countable on one hand (verified in m01/m04 against the RCVS register rather than assumed here). A request for ten firms inside that boundary is almost certainly unsatisfiable on the geography as written; the honest output is a validated count of what exists, plus widenings the rep can approve. This pack therefore treats "Orkney" as the rep's centre of gravity, reports exactly what is there, and reports the adjacent bands (Highlands and Islands, Scottish farm-animal and mixed practice, UK veterinary groups with a central client-contact team) as findings — not as a decision to widen.

**Second, the product's floor is a contact centre, not a reception desk.** Insights360 is built for operations running between 5 and 250 contact-centre seats, and the knowledge set's own exclusion list names sub-5-seat operations as out of profile because £4.99/seat against a £1,280 setup fee does not work for either side. A single-site island veterinary practice with two people answering the phone is below that floor. The kinds of buyer this pack can legitimately carry are therefore veterinary *organisations* where phone handling has been concentrated: out-of-hours providers, multi-site groups with a central client-care line, referral hospitals with a bookings team, and corporate groups running a shared contact centre. Whether any of those sit in or serve Orkney is the research question.

## The spine

The argument that holds across every kind of buyer here is coverage, not price. Manual call review in a veterinary setting is either non-existent or anecdotal: a practice manager hears one call in a hundred, usually because a client complained about it. Every call the pipeline ingests is transcribed and scored against the customer's own QA rules, which turns "we think the phones are fine" into a measured pass rate with call-level evidence. Price is the enabler that makes this reachable below the enterprise floor, and it is an offer-stage detail, not the opening line.

## What is being displaced

The incumbent practice is not a competing vendor. It is (a) no call review at all, (b) a practice manager or head nurse listening to a handful of recordings when a complaint lands, and (c) client-satisfaction inference from review sites and post-visit surveys rather than from the conversation itself. In the larger veterinary groups the incumbent may be a CCaaS platform's bundled quality module or a mystery-shopper call audit bought as a service. The displacement claim is sampling: a human listening to a few calls after the fact, versus every ingested call scored the same way.

## Ready now, and what must not lead

Ready now is the post-call loop: ingest from the existing phone system, transcribe, score against the tenant's QA rules, flag configurable risk types, per-agent pages, searchable call explorer, per-call PDF. Automated feeds exist for 3CX, OAK/ClarifyGo and RingCentral; everything else is scoped per customer and must be phrased as "works with recordings from".

What must not lead is longer than usual for this sector, because veterinary buyers will ask for exactly the things that are not shipped: listening to the call in the app, a portal the receptionist logs into, an audit pack for a regulator, automatic deletion after a retention period. Those are all HOLD. The latency wording matters too — "same day" or "within a couple of hours", never "minutes", and hosting is EU (Frankfurt), never "UK only".

## Hypotheses carried in

There are no prior packs for this product in this org, so nothing is inherited. The hypotheses listed below are the research team's own going in, and each is tested in the waves that follow rather than asserted.

m01.body:
## The honest shape of this market

The rep asked for veterinary practices in Orkney. The research answer is that Orkney contains **two veterinary businesses across four premises**, and the Scottish Government's own list of island practices participating in the Highlands and Islands Veterinary Services Scheme names them: Northvet Veterinary Group (Junction Road, Kirkwall and Lamaquoy, Harray) and Flett and Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons (Hatston, Kirkwall). A consumer comparison site filtered to a fifteen-mile radius of Kirkwall lists four premises, which reconciles: Northvet holds three of them. That is the whole universe inside the brief's geography, and it is two firms against a request for ten.

So the landscape this pack maps is deliberately two-layered. The inner layer is Orkney itself, where the only question is whether either business clears the product's seat floor. It does, at least once: Northvet's own business-directory entry lists nine reception and administration staff alongside nine veterinary surgeons, three veterinary nurses, an animal nursing assistant, a student nurse and a practice manager — which puts concentrated phone handling at or above the five-seat floor the knowledge set sets as the commercial minimum. The outer layer is the set of veterinary *structures* elsewhere in Great Britain where phone handling has actually been concentrated into something recognisable as a contact centre. That is where the product's 5-to-250-seat band is comfortably met, and the pack reports those as findings so the campaign agent can see what a widening would buy.

## Why now, and it is not a vet-specific phone rule

There is a real regulatory clock, and it is the CMA's, not the RCVS's. The CMA closed its market investigation into veterinary services for household pets on 24 March 2026, the statutory deadline for putting the substantive Order in place is 23 September 2026, and compliance dates then fall in December 2026 for larger businesses and March 2027 for smaller ones — where "smaller" is defined on the CMA's own guidance page as fewer than fifteen first-opinion practices, which makes every Orkney firm a small business with the longer runway. Two of the six remedy categories bear directly on what gets said on the telephone: providing general information on ownership, prices and services, and managing complaints. The CMA also states plainly that the veterinary business will need written policies and processes so that vets and nurses can act in line with the relevant RCVS codes, and that this might include additional training on communications with pet owners.

That is the wedge, and it needs stating carefully (inference): the CMA does not require anyone to monitor or analyse phone calls. What it does is turn "what we tell clients about price, ownership, options and how to complain" into a written-policy obligation with a compliance date and a financial-penalty backstop, and the telephone is where most of that telling happens. The honest product claim is evidence that the policy is actually being followed on calls, not a compliance pack — the facts file is explicit that regulator-ready evidence packs are not built.

## Where the real seats are

The veterinary phone estate is more concentrated than the practice estate. Vets Now runs a named Contact Centre in Dunfermline with call handlers on published hourly rates, supporting both its own out-of-hours service and IVC's daytime clinics; that is an operation with a shift pattern, team leaders and a recruitment cadence. Equicomms, a specialist veterinary out-of-hours answering service, states on its own site that it runs eighteen call handlers supporting over sixty clinics — squarely inside the 5-to-250 band, and staffed by veterinary nurses rather than generic operators, which makes call quality a professional rather than a commercial question for them. Goddard Veterinary Group advertises for a "Client Support Centre Call Handler", which names the same structure inside an independent multi-site group. Those three shapes — the emergency provider, the specialist bureau, the group's central client-care line — are where the product's band is met without argument.

The corporate layer above them is real but mostly out of profile. Six groups dominate UK first-opinion practice, and a community-maintained map puts IVC Evidensia at 910 practices, VetPartners at 485, Vets4Pets at 483, CVS Group at 418, Medivet at 354 and Linnaeus at 224. CVS's own site says it operates around 500 practices including forty dedicated out-of-hours sites. Any centralised contact operation at that scale is likely to breach the 250-seat ceiling and would certainly want the group-level cross-tenant view the facts file says does not exist and is not on the roadmap.

## What the sector measures, and what it does not

The profession has hard numbers on complaints and almost none on calls. The Veterinary Client Mediation Service, funded by the RCVS, received 3,548 enquiries in 2023-24 and more than 3,600 in 2025; customer service accounted for 19% of complaints, with service and communication around consent the fastest-rising sub-category at +31%. That is the closest thing to a public dataset on where veterinary client relationships break, and the answer is communication. On call volumes the published evidence is thin and old: the best figure found is Alison Lambert's In Practice paper stating that 99% of initial client contact happens on the telephone and that a one-vet equine practice averages 400 inbound calls a month. A practice manager reading this pack's language should recognise both halves.

The next six months are unusually legible because the CMA published a timetable. What is not legible is whether veterinary practices record their client calls at all — and that, not seat count, is the gating question for this product, because Insights360 analyses recordings the customer's own phone system makes. It is logged as an unknown, not papered over.

bodies.name: Competition and Markets Authority
bodies.role: Competition regulator; ran the veterinary services market investigation and will impose the binding Order
bodies.relevance: Owns the only hard dated clock in this sector: Order by 23 September 2026, larger businesses complying December 2026, smaller ones March 2027, with financial penalties for breach. Two of its six remedy categories are about what clients are told and how complaints are handled.

bodies.name: Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons (RCVS)
bodies.role: Statutory regulator of vets and veterinary nurses; maintains the register of veterinary practice premises and runs the Practice Standards Scheme
bodies.relevance: Takes on a new CMA-mandated monitoring role funded by a levy on veterinary businesses, and runs the Practice Standards Scheme whose Client Service Award rests on a single Client Experience module. Its supporting guidance on communication and consent and on clinical and client records is the professional standard a call would be judged against.

bodies.name: Veterinary Client Mediation Service (VCMS)
bodies.role: RCVS-funded independent alternative dispute resolution service for veterinary complaints, delivered by Nockolds

bodies.role: Trade body for practising vets and practice owners; runs Congress and a CMA-focused technology roadshow

bodies.role: Representative body for veterinary practice managers and leaders; runs VMG Congress
bodies.relevance: The practice-manager constituency is the champion role for this product, and VMG is its organising body. It is running a practice-management research survey specifically on the operational and people-management reality managers face.

bodies.name: Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)
bodies.relevance: Sets the rules on both sides of this campaign: whether a cold email to a veterinary practice is lawful, and what a practice must do to record and retain client calls at all. bodies.name: British Veterinary Association (BVA)
bodies.role: Representative body for the veterinary profession; runs the Voice of the Veterinary Profession survey
bodies.relevance: Publishes the profession's own evidence on client behaviour, including that 57% of vets in clinical practice were intimidated by clients, which is the professional-wellbeing framing of a call-quality problem.

claims.text: The CMA groups its veterinary remedies into six categories: general information on ownership, prices and services; information and policies on treatments; prescribing veterinary medicines; managing out-of-hours contracts; offering cremation services; and managing complaints. The remedies apply mainly to veterinary businesses operating one or more first-opinion practices, and do not apply to charitable small-animal providers.

The CMA states that the veterinary business will need written policies and processes to ensure vets and vet nurses can act in line with relevant RCVS Codes and Guidance, for example on providing impartial advice and timely information about treatment options and prices, and that this might include additional training on communications with pet owners. Non-compliance can result in directions or a financial penalty.
claims.quote: The veterinary business where you work will need to have written policies and processes to ensure that vets and vet nurses are able to act in line with relevant parts of the RCVS Codes and Guidance... This might include additional training on communications with pet owners.

claims.text: The CMA defines smaller veterinary businesses as those with fewer than fifteen first-opinion practices and larger businesses as those with fifteen or more, and says smaller businesses generally have more time to comply.

Northvet Veterinary Group's Kirkwall business-directory entry lists 9 veterinary surgeons, 3 veterinary nurses, an animal nursing assistant, a student veterinary nurse, a practice manager and 9 reception/administration staff, across three branch surgeries covering all of Orkney including the outer isles, with a 24-hour emergency service 365 days a year. Its own recruitment advertising describes a 12-vet team.

Equicomms, an out-of-hours call-handling service for veterinary practices started four years before the page was read, states on its own site that it has 18 call handlers and supports over 60 clinics, and that all its staff are veterinary nurses, equine veterinary nurses or equine veterinary technicians.

Vets Now describes itself as the UK's leading provider of emergency veterinary services and says it provides emergency out-of-hours care for over 1,400 clinics in the UK, operating a Contact Centre in Dunfermline whose call handlers are the first point of contact for clients and follow established call-handling protocols.

Six corporate groups dominate UK first-opinion veterinary practice. A community-maintained consolidator list puts IVC Evidensia at 910 practices, VetPartners at 485, Vets4Pets at 483, CVS Group at 418, Medivet at 354 and Linnaeus at 224. CVS Group's own site states it has 500 veterinary practices in the UK and Australia including nine specialist-led referral hospitals and 40 dedicated out-of-hours sites.

The VCMS 2023-24 Insight Report records 3,548 enquiries, with standards of care at 60% of complaints, customer service at 19% (service and communication around consent up 31%) and clinical fees at 14%. It invited 1,050 practices into mediation, 77% accepted, and 767 mediated cases achieved an 82% resolution rate. A later VCMS statement says more than 3,600 enquiries were received in 2025 with over 80% of referred complaints resolved.

claims.text: The CMA cites as its primary concern that average prices of vet services rose by 63% between 2016 and 2023, and its market investigation attracted 56,000 responses to its Call for Information and over 450 stakeholder responses on the Provisional Decision.

The RCVS Practice Standards Scheme awards include a Client Service Award, presented to practices demonstrating high levels of care for their clients, which rests on a single module called Client Experience covering the practical and behavioural steps practices can take to improve client service.

triggers.text: The CMA published the final report of its market investigation into veterinary services for household pets on 24 March 2026, confirming a package of remedies grouped into six categories, two of which concern information given to pet owners and the management of complaints.
The CMA's statutory deadline for implementing remedial action, by making the substantive Order and accepting the RCVS Undertaking, is 23 September 2026 — twelve days after this pack was written.

On 20 August 2026 the CMA published the final Veterinary Services Market Investigation (Funding) Order 2026 and the RCVS Funding Undertakings, establishing a levy on veterinary businesses, set by the number of first-opinion practices owned, to fund the RCVS's new compliance-monitoring role.

Compliance dates split by size: for the information-on-ownership-prices-and-services remedies the Order is made September 2026, larger businesses comply December 2026, and smaller businesses — those with fewer than fifteen first-opinion practices — comply March 2027, with the RCVS modifying Find a Vet by June 2027 and businesses providing data to the RCVS by September 2027.

SPVS is running an online 'Smarter Practice Tech Day' on Wednesday 21 October 2026 explicitly to show practices how technology can help them implement the CMA remedies, improve client communication and transparency, and make better use of data, with a supplier directory supplement included in registration.

Northvet Veterinary Group Ltd is advertising for an experienced mixed or farm-animal veterinary surgeon to join its 12-vet team in Orkney, with a closing date of 25 September 2026, because a colleague is leaving to travel overseas; the advert names Lynn Wilson as Practice Manager as the contact.

Vets Now is recruiting full-time and part-time call handlers into its Dunfermline Contact Centre, supporting IVC daytime clinics as well as its own out-of-hours service, with an available start date of Monday 12 October and a published rate of GBP 13.45 per hour rising to GBP 15.60 on the enhanced night rate.

The Scottish Government updated its published list of HIVSS participating island practices on 31 July 2026, which is the most recent confirmation that both Orkney veterinary businesses remain in the scheme.

The UK Government published a White Paper, 'Our Vision for a Thriving Veterinary Sector', reported by the VCMS on 9 July 2026 as a milestone in reform of veterinary regulation and consumer protection; the CMA's final report had recommended a new Veterinary Surgeons Act bringing veterinary businesses, not just individuals, into regulatory scope.

marketSize: UK veterinary services industry revenue is put at GBP 7.3 billion for 2026, growing at 4.8% a year since 2020, across approximately 3,560 registered veterinary services businesses.
The RCVS Find a Vet practice directory returns 3,567 RCVS-accredited veterinary practices, and the RCVS states that 65% of UK practices have earned Practice Standards Scheme accreditation.

The Scottish Government's list of island practices participating in the Highlands and Islands Veterinary Services Scheme names two veterinary businesses covering Orkney mainland and adjacent islands: Northvet Veterinary Group (two listed addresses, Harray and Kirkwall) and Flett and Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons (Kirkwall). The page was last updated 31 July 2026.

A consumer price-comparison listing for Kirkwall, filtered to a fifteen-mile radius, lists four veterinary premises: Northvet Veterinary Group at Junction Road, Lammaquoy and North End Road, and Flett & Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons at Hatston. Consultation fees shown are from GBP 51.50 (Northvet Junction Road) and from GBP 46.18 (Flett & Carmichael).
31,224 veterinary surgeons were on the UK practising register as of 1 January 2025, up from 30,155 a year earlier, alongside 24,952 registered veterinary nurses.

Client behaviour: 57% of vets in clinical practice were intimidated by clients, per BVA's Respect Your Vet Team campaign.
Price trajectory: average prices of vet services rose 63% between 2016 and 2023, the CMA's primary stated concern.
Consultation price on Orkney: from GBP 51.50 at Northvet's Junction Road branch and from GBP 46.18 at Flett & Carmichael, per a consumer comparison listing.

Call-handler pay as a seat-cost proxy: GBP 13.45 per hour standard and GBP 15.60 enhanced night rate at a named veterinary contact centre; a full-time call handler post is advertised at GBP 26,227.50.

m03.body:
## Four situations, not four job titles

The brief names a sector and a place. What actually determines whether this product fits is a structural question: has the telephone been concentrated into a job that somebody owns? In veterinary services there are four answers to that, and they behave completely differently as buyers.

The first is the one the rep asked for and it is the hardest. **The island mixed practice** has no corporate parent, runs its own 24-hour emergency cover across branches and outer isles, and has a reception and administration team large enough to clear the five-seat floor but small enough that every seat is visible to the practice manager by walking past them. Its compliance date under the CMA Order is March 2027, because it has fewer than fifteen first-opinion practices. Its champion is the practice manager, and the signer is a veterinary-surgeon director who is also seeing clients. The angle that works here is not compliance and it is not price — it is reconstruction: when a client says "I was told on the phone that…", can you find out what was actually said?

The second is the structurally best fit in the whole pack. **The specialist veterinary answering bureau** sells call handling as its entire product, publishes its handler count, staffs with veterinary nurses, and has just had its competitive position changed by a CMA remedy that exists specifically to make it easier for practices to switch out-of-hours supplier. A bureau with eighteen handlers and sixty client clinics has both the seat count and a commercial reason to hold evidence of consistency: its renewal conversations are about trust in call quality, and it currently has nothing to show but testimonials.

The third is the product's textbook tenant. **The multi-site group with a central client-support centre** has already made the organisational decision that concentrates the calls, has a supervisor layer, and has enough volume that a pass rate means something statistically. It is also the most likely of the four to already own a vet-native phone system that records — which removes the gating blocker.

The fourth has the most seats and the most risk. **The emergency provider's contact centre** handles triage calls where the consequence of a mishandled conversation is clinical, not commercial. It has shift patterns, published hourly rates and a team-leader tier. It is also the one most likely to breach the 250-seat ceiling, and the one most likely to sit inside a corporate group that will ask for a view across several entities — which the facts file says does not exist and is not planned.

## What is shared, and what must not be promised

All four share one gating question that comes before seat count: does the phone system record the calls, and does the practice have lawful ground and a retention position for those recordings? Insights360 does not record; it analyses recordings the customer's existing system makes. A veterinary call-recording policy found in the wild lists exactly the purposes a practice already writes down — training needs, staff performance, protecting staff from abusive calls, establishing facts in a complaint, and evidence for a regulatory investigation — and also states that the practice deletes recordings automatically within 30 days. Insights360 has no automated retention or deletion, which is a real conversation, not a footnote.

All four will also ask for three things that are not shipped: to listen to the call in the app, to give the receptionist her own login, and to produce something a regulator would accept. Those are HOLD and they are named as boundaries in m11, not softened.

## Where the deal economics actually land

The honest position is that seat counts are estimates in three of the four cases, because veterinary organisations do not publish them. Only Equicomms publishes a handler count, and only one Orkney practice publishes a reception headcount. Every figure in the deal economics below is the published plan price applied to an estimated or confirmed seat count, and is marked as such; the setup fee and configuration review are fixed and dominate the first-year arithmetic at the small end. For a nine-seat island practice the one-off fees are the deal, not the subscription — which is why the sales cycle for that kind of buyer is long and the champion needs something concrete to take to a director.

claims.text: A multi-site independent veterinary group advertises a 'Veterinary Client Support Centre Call Handler' role, describing it as being the first port of call for clients contacting the Client Support Centre, which evidences the centralised client-call structure as a real organisational form in GB veterinary groups rather than an inference.

A named veterinary emergency provider's Dunfermline contact centre operates a Monday-to-Sunday 08:00-19:00 shift pattern with occasional bank-holiday working, publishes a standard rate of GBP 13.45 per hour and an enhanced night rate of GBP 15.60, advertises a separate Team Leader post at GBP 33,167.97 and a Customer Relations Consultant post at GBP 26,489 pro rata, and runs rolling intakes with fixed start dates.

A published GB veterinary practice call-recording policy states that recordings may be used to investigate compliance with the practice's call quality standards, to provide further training, to support the investigation of complaints, to ensure the practice complies with regulatory procedures and to provide evidence for any regulatory investigation — and that recordings will be automatically deleted within 30 days.

The Orkney island practice archetype is grounded in a real structure: Northvet operates three branch surgeries covering all of Orkney including the outer isles, provides a 24-hour emergency service 365 days a year with clients told to call as normal out of hours, employs around nine reception and administration staff alongside a practice manager, and appears on the Scottish Government's HIVSS participating island practices list updated 31 July 2026.

RCVS supporting guidance on communication and consent states that practice staff may be the first to become aware of any misunderstanding by clients concerning a procedure or treatment, and that vets and nurses should advise practice staff to communicate any concerns to the senior veterinary surgeon and ensure the client is kept fully informed — which places a professional expectation on what non-clinical staff notice and pass on from client conversations.

The expected buying committee for this product is 2-4 stakeholders — a QA or compliance champion, operations sign-off and a finance or IT review — rather than an enterprise RFP committee, which matches the role structures found in all four veterinary archetypes.

archetypes.name: The island mixed practice running its own emergency line

roles.needs: Something she can act on without adding a listening task to her own week. She already owns the complaints procedure, the rota and the reception team; what she does not have is any measurement of the phones beyond what clients tell her. She needs the CMA written-policy work to produce evidence rather than just a document, and she needs the per-call PDF to take into a difficult conversation with a client or a team member.
roles.title: Practice Manager
roles.seniority: Senior manager, reports to the director group

roles.needs: A number that justifies a one-off fee on an island practice's P&L. Will ask what happens to the recordings, who can see them, how long they are kept, and whether the team will feel surveilled. Wants the boundary statements up front — post-call only, nothing during a consultation, no agent logins — because the clinical team's trust matters more than the tool.
roles.title: Veterinary Surgeon Director / Practice Principal

roles.needs: A fair basis for coaching. Currently coaches on what she happened to overhear. Needs the same rule applied to every call so that a new starter and a fifteen-year veteran are assessed the same way, and needs to be able to point at a specific call rather than say 'you sometimes sound rushed'. Must be given a supervisor role, not an admin role, because data visibility is not role-gated but settings writes are.
roles.title: Head Receptionist / Senior Client Care Coordinator

archetypes.situation: An independent, RCVS-accredited mixed practice on a Scottish island group, serving pets, farm animals and horses across two or three branch surgeries plus the outer isles, with no corporate parent and no out-of-hours provider to hand the phone to — clients are told to call the practice as normal at night and a dedicated emergency team responds. Reception and administration is a concentrated team of around nine people handling everything from appointment booking to farm emergency triage to medicine orders. The practice participates in the Scottish Government's Highlands and Islands Veterinary Services Scheme. Under the CMA Order it is a 'smaller business' (fewer than fifteen first-opinion practices), so its compliance date for the transparency remedies is March 2027, and it is about to need written policies on what clients are told about prices, ownership, treatment options and how to complain. Its calls are long-relationship calls in a community where the practice has traded since the nineteenth century and a complaint is a social event, not a ticket.
archetypes.sizeRange: Approximately 9 reception and administration seats alongside 9-12 veterinary surgeons, 3-4 nurses and a practice manager; 1-3 premises

dominantPain.text: When a client disputes what they were told on the phone — about a price, a treatment option, or when to bring the animal in — the practice has no way to establish what was actually said, so the dispute is settled on memory and goodwill. The published complaint data for the sector shows customer service is 19% of all veterinary complaints and that service and communication around consent is the fastest-rising sub-category, up 31%, while a veterinary call-recording policy found in the wild names 'establish the facts in the event of a complaint either by a client, or a member of staff and so assist in resolving it' as an explicit purpose of recording at all.
dominantPain.quote: Establish the facts in the event of a complaint either by a client, or a member of staff and so assist in resolving it.
dominantPain.speaker: Wilson's Veterinary Practice

archetypes.openingAngle: A client told you something different from what your team remembers saying. Right now that is unresolvable. Every call your phone system records can be transcribed and scored against your own rules, so the next time it happens you are reading the conversation rather than reconstructing it — and your March 2027 CMA policy work produces evidence, not just a document.

dealEconomics.note: Seat count is estimated from a published staff mix (9 reception/administration staff at one Orkney practice); no veterinary practice publishes a phone-seat count. The one-off fees are the binding commercial constraint at this size and must be stated openly.
dealEconomics.plan: Starter at GBP 4.99 per seat per month with 40 pooled hours, or Professional at GBP 7.99 with 70 hours if call volume runs high across branches and an emergency line
dealEconomics.seatRange: 5-10 seats (reception and administration, plus the practice manager and a supervisor)
dealEconomics.budgetLine: Practice operating costs, most plausibly alongside the CMA compliance work or the existing telephony spend; there is no existing QA line to displace
dealEconomics.salesCycle: Long. Two decision-makers, an owner-director who is also consulting, and no internal precedent for buying analytics. Expect the CMA March 2027 date to set the pace rather than any urgency of ours.
dealEconomics.yearOneValue: Dominated by the one-off fees: GBP 1,280 setup plus GBP 640 configuration review around month one, with the monthly subscription a small fraction of that at this seat count (derived from the published plan prices and an estimated 5-10 seats — not a quote)

archetypes.name: The specialist veterinary answering bureau whose product is the call

roles.needs: Coverage across every shift, not a sample, because the shifts nobody watches are the night shifts. Needs a pass rate she can put in a client review pack, and rule-failure patterns that tell her whether a problem is one handler or the whole call-flow design. Needs the calls explorer filters — by handler, by category, by sentiment, by risk — because her questions are always 'which calls, not how many'.
roles.title: Operations Manager / Service Delivery Manager

roles.needs: A commercial argument tied to retention and to winning practices from the generic messaging services. Will be acutely aware of the CMA switching remedy and of the need to look more accountable than a competitor. Will also want to know whether showing a client practice its own call scores is possible — which must be answered carefully, because there is no cross-tenant or group view.
roles.title: Founder / Managing Director

roles.needs: Coaching points she did not have to write herself, attached to the specific call, so a handover brief takes minutes rather than an evening. Needs the needs-review list to tell her which of last night's calls to look at first. Must be told plainly that the list is a list, not a workflow — there is no assignment, no status and no SLA tracking.
roles.title: Shift Supervisor / Senior Call Handler

archetypes.situation: A small GB business whose entire service is answering veterinary practices' telephones — typically out of hours, sometimes overflow in hours — staffed by people with veterinary training rather than generic operators, working to a call-flow menu agreed with each client practice and escalating to the on-call vet. One such bureau publishes eighteen call handlers supporting over sixty clinics. Its value proposition is triage quality and the calming of distressed owners, and its proof today is client testimonials. From September 2026 the CMA's out-of-hours remedies restrict contract terms for third-party out-of-hours suppliers specifically to make switching easier for first-opinion practices, which converts a sticky contract base into a contestable one. The bureau's own blind spot is identical to its clients': it has no systematic record of how its handlers actually performed on the thousands of calls nobody reviewed.
archetypes.sizeRange: 10-30 call handlers plus one or two supervisors; serving 20-100 client practices

dominantPain.role: Client of a veterinary answering service
dominantPain.text: The bureau's whole differentiator is that its handlers are clinically trained and triage properly, but it cannot demonstrate that consistently across handlers, shifts or client practices — its published evidence is a page of testimonials. When a client practice's on-call vet complains that a call was escalated badly, or that a non-urgent call should have been filtered, the bureau is arguing about one remembered call. Its own marketing makes the claim that filtering 'reduces the number of non-urgent or routine calls that would take up valuable time of the clinical out-of-hours teams', which is a measurable claim it currently cannot measure.
dominantPain.quote: Your staff filtering the calls using the agreed call-flow menu helps reduce the number of non-urgent or routine calls that would take up valuable time of the clinical out-of-hours teams trying to prioritise inpatients and urgent referrals only.
dominantPain.speaker: Unnamed client practice, quoted by Kernow Vets Messaging

archetypes.openingAngle: Your handlers are veterinary nurses and that is your whole case against a generic messaging service. The calls that prove it are the ones nobody listened to. Every call your system records can be scored against your own call-flow rules, so consistency across night shifts becomes something you show a client practice at renewal rather than something you assert.

dealEconomics.note: One bureau publishes 18 call handlers; the 12-30 range generalises from that single confirmed figure and is an estimate. Pooled-hour consumption is the real unknown for a 24-hour operation and must be scoped, not assumed.
dealEconomics.plan: Professional at GBP 7.99 per seat per month with 70 pooled hours, or Enterprise at GBP 9.99 with 100 hours given continuous out-of-hours call volume; overage at GBP 0.50 per analysed hour beyond the pooled allowance is the variable to watch
dealEconomics.seatRange: 12-30 seats (call handlers plus supervisors; agents are not users, so handler seats are counted for licensing of supervisors and managers — confirm how the tenant wants to licence)
dealEconomics.budgetLine: Cost of service delivery or quality assurance; plausibly justified against retention rather than efficiency
dealEconomics.salesCycle: Shorter than the practice. One owner, one operations manager, a clear commercial trigger, and no clinical-governance committee. The binding question is telephony: a bureau is likely to run a cloud phone system, and whether it is 3CX, OAK/ClarifyGo or RingCentral decides whether the feed is automated or scoped.
dealEconomics.yearOneValue: Monthly subscription becomes material at this seat count and the GBP 1,280 setup plus GBP 640 configuration review are absorbed more easily than at practice scale (derived from the published plan prices and an estimated 12-30 seats — not a quote)

archetypes.name: The multi-site independent group that centralised its client calls

roles.needs: One scorecard applied to the whole central team, period-over-period comparison so she can show movement, and rule-failure patterns that separate a training problem from a process problem. Will immediately ask for a per-branch or per-team breakdown — which must be answered honestly: one scorecard per tenant, no team entities in the interface, no per-team scorecard.
roles.title: Head of Client Experience / Client Support Centre Manager

roles.needs: Margin-defensible pricing and a defensible answer on CMA compliance across every branch. Wants to know what the tool replaces; the answer is a sampling habit and a spreadsheet, not a vendor. Will test the data-residency and security answers, which is where EU (Frankfurt) hosting, the ISO 27001 group certificate and the internally audited tenant isolation belong.
roles.title: Operations Director / Group Operations Manager

roles.needs: A prioritised list of calls worth reviewing and coaching points already drafted, because she is handling calls herself for part of the shift. Needs per-agent pages to prepare a one-to-one. Must be told that coaching notes are read-only, copied out rather than edited in place.
roles.title: Client Support Team Leader

archetypes.situation: An independent veterinary group of roughly five to fourteen first-opinion practices that has already taken the calls off the branch front desks and put them into a named central team — advertised in its own recruitment as a 'Client Support Centre' or 'Client Care' team. One group advertises for a highly experienced call handler to be 'the first port of call for our valued clients'. The group has a hospital or flagship site open around the clock, a supervisor layer, and enough aggregate call volume that a pass rate is statistically meaningful. It is still a 'smaller business' under the CMA definition, so March 2027 is its transparency deadline, and it has to make one written policy work identically across every branch — which is exactly what a shared scorecard does. It is also the archetype most likely to have bought a vet-native phone system that already records and transcribes, which removes the gating blocker and raises the 'we already have this' objection.
archetypes.sizeRange: 10-40 client-support seats across a group of roughly 5-14 first-opinion practices

dominantPain.role: Author, Vet Times customer-service feature (role not stated on the page)
dominantPain.text: Centralising the calls was supposed to make the client experience consistent, and nobody can tell whether it did. The group's own sector guidance says consistency comes from shared scripts, templates and tone guidelines reducing variation across every touchpoint — but a script is an input, not a measurement, and the group has no way to see whether the team applied it on a Tuesday afternoon. Meanwhile the client-facing failure mode most often named is a client having to repeat themselves to different individuals because context was not passed on.
dominantPain.quote: A major cause of frustration for clients is having to repeat themselves to different individuals. Ensuring everyone on the team has access to the same information and ensuring context is given when tasks are passed between individuals is vital to delivering a great customer experience.
dominantPain.speaker: Oli Viner

archetypes.openingAngle: You centralised the calls to make the client experience the same everywhere. Your shared scripts say what should happen; nothing tells you what did. Every call the system records can be scored against one rule set, so 'consistent' becomes a pass rate with the failing rule named — which is also the evidence your March 2027 CMA policy work will need.

dealEconomics.note: No GB veterinary group publishes its client-support-centre headcount; the 12-40 range is an estimate inferred from the existence of a named central team across multiple branches. Confirm on the first call.
dealEconomics.plan: Professional at GBP 7.99 per seat per month with 70 pooled hours as the likely landing point; Enterprise at GBP 9.99 with 100 hours where group call volume is high
dealEconomics.budgetLine: Group operations or client-experience budget; possibly the CMA compliance programme
dealEconomics.salesCycle: Medium. Two or three stakeholders — client-experience champion, operations sign-off, an IT or telephony check — matching the knowledge set's 2-4 stakeholder expectation. The decisive technical question is which phone platform the central team runs.
dealEconomics.yearOneValue: The best commercial fit of the four: monthly subscription at 12-40 seats comfortably carries the GBP 1,280 setup and GBP 640 configuration review, with no seat minimum and no annual commitment reducing the approval threshold (derived from the published plan prices and an estimated 12-40 seats — not a quote)

archetypes.name: The emergency provider's triage contact centre

roles.needs: Volume and quality at a glance with period-over-period comparison, and a drill-through from a dashboard count to the actual calls. Needs to know which protocol step fails most often across a rolling intake. Will ask for automatic anomaly callouts; they are not built.
roles.title: Contact Centre Manager

roles.needs: Assurance that triage risk is being surfaced systematically rather than anecdotally, and a defensible position on how recordings and transcripts are handled. This is the role most likely to ask for regulator-ready evidence packs and for the ability to listen to the moment that produced a flag — neither of which exists, and both of which must be refused plainly.
roles.title: Clinical Governance Lead / Head of Clinical Standards

roles.needs: Per-handler trend pages to run development conversations, and a prioritised review list for the previous night. Wants to assign calls to reviewers and track them to resolution; there is no assignment, no status workflow and no SLA tracking, so this must be set as a manual habit rather than a product feature.
roles.title: Contact Centre Team Leader
roles.seniority: Team lead, on a distinct salary band

archetypes.situation: A veterinary emergency and out-of-hours provider running a named contact centre as a distinct operation — a physical site, published hourly rates and an enhanced night rate, a seven-day 08:00-19:00 shift pattern on the daytime side, team leaders on separate salary bands, and rolling intakes with fixed start dates. One such operator states it provides emergency out-of-hours care for over 1,400 UK clinics and that its call handlers are the first point of contact, logging call details and following established call-handling protocols. The calls are clinical triage under emotional pressure: the handler is deciding, in effect, how fast a distressed owner gets to a vet. Referral teaching hospitals run a smaller version of the same thing, with an out-of-hours emergency care team taking the call and advising the owner. This is the highest-consequence call estate in the sector and the one where 'we reviewed a sample' is least defensible.
archetypes.sizeRange: Unverified; large enough to run shift patterns and a team-leader tier. May exceed the 250-seat ceiling at the largest operator, in which case it is out of profile

dominantPain.text: Handlers follow established call-handling protocols and escalate complex queries, but compliance with those protocols is not measured on the calls themselves — only inferred from outcomes and from the calls that went wrong loudly enough to be noticed. On a seven-day 08:00-19:00 pattern plus enhanced-rate night shifts, the shifts with the least supervision are the ones with the highest-acuity calls, and a rolling intake of new handlers with fixed start dates means there is always a cohort whose protocol adherence nobody has verified.

archetypes.openingAngle: Your handlers follow established call-handling protocols. On a seven-day pattern with enhanced night rates and rolling new intakes, nobody can see whether the protocol held on the calls that mattered. Every call your system records can be scored against those protocol steps after it ends, with the failing step named and the high-risk calls listed.

dealEconomics.note: Pricing facts are live and confirmed, but no seat count, call volume or analysed-hours figure could be established for any GB veterinary emergency contact centre. Treat every commercial number for this kind of buyer as unconfirmed until the first call, and qualify the 250-seat ceiling before anything else.
dealEconomics.plan: Enterprise at GBP 9.99 per seat per month with 100 pooled hours is the only plausible plan at this volume, with GBP 0.50 per hour overage likely to be the dominant line on a 24-hour operation
dealEconomics.seatRange: Unknown. Must be sized before anything else, because above 250 seats this is out of profile
dealEconomics.salesCycle: Longest of the four, and the most likely to fail on constraints rather than price. Clinical governance sign-off, an information-security review that will probe SSO, redaction and retention, and a parent group that may want a cross-entity view.
dealEconomics.yearOneValue: Not estimable without a seat count and an analysed-hours forecast; pooled-hour overage, not seats, would drive the bill

m04.body:
## How the lists were filtered, and what that produced

Every seed below was found by filtering a register or a list to fit before choosing, never by taking a default order. For Orkney that meant the Scottish Government's HIVSS participating-island-practices table filtered to the rows whose 'Island' column reads Orkney — four rows, two distinct businesses — cross-checked against a consumer comparison listing filtered to a fifteen-mile radius of Kirkwall, which returns four premises and reconciles to the same two businesses. That is the entire Orkney universe and it is two firms, not ten. The rep's number cannot be met inside the brief's geography, and the pack says so rather than padding.

For the three non-Orkney kinds of buyer the filter was structural rather than geographic: organisations that publish evidence of a concentrated call-handling function — a published handler count, a named contact centre, or a live vacancy for a client-support-centre call handler. That filter is deliberately narrow because the product's floor is five seats and the knowledge set excludes anything below it. It also means the seed list is small: ten firms across four kinds of buyer, of which three have a confirmed or estimated size with a source and the rest are honestly marked unknown.

## What makes a signal here, and what does not

The strongest firm-level signals in veterinary services are recruitment and regulatory. Recruitment works because a live vacancy for a call handler or client-care role is dated, public and specific to the organisation: it proves the function exists, proves it is under strain, and names the closing date. Regulatory works because the CMA Order is the one dated clock everybody in the sector shares, and it is stratified by size, so a buyer's compliance date is derivable from its practice count.

What does not count as a signal, and has been excluded: a practice having a website, a practice offering out-of-hours cover (every UK practice must, by law), a good Google rating, or a vendor's customer logo. Two things were looked for and not found, and are recorded as unknowns rather than manufactured: any public evidence that a named GB veterinary organisation records its client calls, and any published seat count for a veterinary contact centre.

## The recipes, and a warning about titles

The titles in each recipe are real titles observed in GB veterinary job adverts and team pages — Practice Manager, Client Support Centre Manager, Operations Manager, Head of Client Experience, Clinical Governance Lead. Two exclusions matter more than the inclusions. First, never target a receptionist, call handler or veterinary nurse in their agent capacity: there is no agent login and the facts file forbids outreach to agents. A head receptionist or senior client-care coordinator is in scope as a supervisor-level user, not as an agent. Second, never target a veterinary surgeon in their clinical capacity; the practitioner titles in scope are owner-director and clinical-director roles, because those are the signing roles in an independent practice.

One more constraint the campaign agent must carry into lead generation: the ICO treats sole traders and some partnerships as individuals under PECR, and several veterinary practices trade as partnerships. 'Flett and Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons' reads as a partnership name and its premises is listed as 'Hatston Veterinary Centre Ltd' on a comparison site — a discrepancy that must be resolved from Companies House before any email is sent, because it decides whether consent is required. That is a contact-rule consequence of the targeting, and it is detailed in m12.

claims.text: Filtering the Scottish Government's HIVSS participating-island-practices table to its Orkney rows returns four entries resolving to two distinct veterinary businesses, and a consumer comparison listing filtered to a fifteen-mile radius of Kirkwall returns four premises resolving to the same two businesses. There is no third veterinary business in the Orkney Islands council area on any source read this run.

No public evidence was found that either Orkney veterinary business, or any of the other eight seed organisations, records its client telephone calls. The only GB veterinary call-recording policies found in the open were at unrelated practices. Because Insights360 analyses recordings the customer's existing phone system makes and does not record calls itself, this is the binding qualification question for every seed in this module and it cannot be resolved from public sources.

One Orkney seed trades under a partnership-style name, Flett and Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons, while a comparison listing records the premises as 'Hatston Veterinary Centre Ltd'; the other is explicitly a limited company, Northvet Veterinary Group Ltd. This distinction is material to contact rules because the ICO treats sole traders and some partnerships as individuals under PECR, requiring consent or the soft opt-in, while any corporate body including a Scottish partnership or limited liability partnership may be emailed without PECR consent.

The RCVS states, in a notice dated 25 August 2026, that technical updates to its Find a Vet service mean some information will not be available in the short term. Any list built from Find a Vet during this period should be cross-checked against the practice's own website or the Scottish Government scheme list.

## What are the rules on electronic mail marketing?

The rules on electronic mail marketing are in regulation 22. In short, you must not send electronic mail marketing to individuals, unless:

- they have specifically consented to electronic mail from you; or
- they are an existing customer who bought (or negotiated to buy) a similar product or service from you in the past, and you gave them a simple way to opt out both when you first collected their details and in every message you have sent.

You must not disguise or conceal your identity, and you must provide a valid contact address so they can opt out or unsubscribe.

## What about texts and other types of electronic message?

This same rule applies to emails, texts, picture messages, video messages, voicemails, direct messages via social media or any similar message that is stored electronically.

The term ‘electronic mail’ has an intentionally broad meaning that includes new forms of messaging. It is defined as:

> “any text, voice, sound or image message sent over a public electronic communications network which can be stored in the network or in the recipient’s terminal equipment until it is collected by the recipient and includes messages sent using a short message service”.

## What is a ‘soft opt-in’?

The term ‘soft opt-in’ is sometimes used to describe the rule about existing customers. The idea is that if an individual bought something from you recently, gave you their details, and did not opt out of marketing messages, they are probably happy to receive marketing from you about similar products or services even if they haven’t specifically consented. However, you must have given them a clear chance to opt out – both when you first collected their details, and in every message you send.

The soft opt-in rule means you may be able to email or text your own customers, but it does not apply to prospective customers or new contacts (eg from bought-in lists). It also does not apply to non-commercial promotions (eg charity fundraising or political campaigning).

## Is there a text or email version of the TPS?

No. There is no equivalent email or text preference service. This is because you may only send emails or texts to individuals if you have their specific consent or have already offered them an opt-out, so this type of central opt-out register shouldn’t be needed.

## When can we email or text individuals?

You can email or text an individual if they have specifically consented to receiving emails or texts from you – for example, by ticking an opt-in box. See [What counts as consent?](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/guide-to-pecr/electronic-and-telephone-marketing/#consent "Electronic and telephone marketing")

You can also email or text an existing customer who has bought (or discussed buying) a similar product or service from you in the past – but only if you gave them a clear chance to opt out of getting marketing emails or texts when you collected their details, and in every message.

## When can we email or text businesses?

Sole traders and some partnerships are treated as individuals – so you can only email or text them if they have specifically consented, or if they bought a similar product from you in the past and didn’t opt out from marketing messages when you gave them that chance.

You can email or text any corporate body (a company, Scottish partnership, limited liability partnership or government body). However, it is good practice – and good business sense – to keep a ‘do not email or text’ list of any businesses that object or opt out, and screen any new marketing lists against that.

You may also need to consider data protection implications if you are emailing employees at a corporate body who have personal corporate email addresses (eg firstname.lastname@org.co.uk).

For more information, see our separate guidance on [business-to-business marketing](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/business-to-business-marketing/ "Business-to-business marketing").

## Do these rules apply to viral marketing?

Yes – you must comply if you send a marketing message, or if you ‘instigate’ someone else to send it.

Some organisations try to get round the rules by asking people to forward a marketing message to their friends. However, you are ‘instigating’ them to send that message, so you must still comply with PECR. (This does not mean you are responsible every time a customer forwards a message without your knowledge – you must have encouraged them to send it.)

# What veterinary businesses and vets need to do following the CMA’s final vets report

What veterinary businesses and veterinary professionals need to know now that the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has published the final report of its vet services market investigation.

From:[Competition and Markets Authority](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/competition-and-markets-authority)Published:24 March 2026

Get emails about this page

Print this page

The Competition and Markets Authority has been [looking into the veterinary services market](https://www.gov.uk/cma-cases/veterinary-services-market-for-pets-review) since September 2023. We have now published our [final report](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/veterinary-services-for-household-pets-final-decision-report) which includes requirements for veterinary businesses (these are called ‘remedies’).

This page explains the parts of our decision that are most relevant to veterinary businesses and veterinary professionals, and when you may need to make changes.

## Summary of changes

The remedies are grouped into 6 categories.

- [**Providing general information on ownership, prices and services**](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#providing-general-information-on-ownership-prices-and-services): information to support pet owners when choosing a FOP
- [**Providing information and policies on treatments**](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#providing-information-and-policies-on-treatments): information to support pet owners when considering treatments in the practice
- [**Prescribing veterinary medicines**](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#prescribing-veterinary-medicines): information and processes to increase competition in the supply of medicines
- [**Managing out-of-hours contracts**](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#managing-out-of-hours-contracts): restrictions on contract terms for third party out-of-hours suppliers, to make it easier for FOPs to switch
- [**Offering cremation services**](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#offering-cremation-services): information to support choice of service after the death of the pet and provision of a basic communal cremation
- [**Managing complaints**](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#managing-complaints): supporting a good complaints process

## Who this applies to

Our remedies mainly apply to veterinary businesses operating one or more first opinion practices (FOPs) to the extent that they are providing veterinary services for household pets, but some also apply to referral centres, out-of-hours providers, and crematoria.

Our remedies will not apply to [charitable organisations providing small animal veterinary services](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#animalcharities).

They do not directly apply to the veterinary professionals employed at vet practices. As an employee you will, however, see changes that may impact your work. For example, you may be required to provide additional information to pet owners during consultations about treatment costs or options for buying medicines.

The veterinary business where you work will need to have written policies and processes to ensure that vets and vet nurses are able to act in line with relevant parts of the RCVS Codes and Guidance (for example, those on providing pet owners with independent and impartial advice, and appropriate and timely information about treatment options and prices). This might include additional training on communications with pet owners.

If veterinary businesses fail to adhere to such policies or put pressure on vets to act in certain ways or sell certain treatments, they could potentially be in breach of the Order. Find out [what happens if a veterinary business does not comply with the Order](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/what-veterinary-businesses-and-vets-need-to-do-following-the-cmas-final-vets-report#what-happens-nextmaking-these-requirements-legally-binding).

## When you need to make changes

The time to comply with these requirements varies by remedy and size of business, with smaller businesses (those with fewer than 15 FOPs) generally having more time than larger businesses (those with 15 FOPs or more).

Our [timetable provides a simple overview](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/69c22cf8cfa346b9d4704af8/Vet_timetable_infographics.pdf) of when you need to make the changes.

## What happens next: making these requirements legally binding

We have started the implementation phase. This means we will now draft a legal document setting out the detail of the requirements. We call this document a CMA Order.  The Order will make the remedies legally binding for the businesses to which it applies. See our descriptions of remedies to check if a remedy applies to your business.

We will continue to engage with the sector as we prepare an initial draft of this Order and we will publicly consult on the draft text. We have set out the timings in our administrative timetable on our [case page](https://www.gov.uk/cma-cases/veterinary-services-market-for-pets-review). We will take consultation responses into account when finalising the Order. We are legally required to complete this phase within 6 months.

Once in place, any veterinary business to which the Order applies will have a legal duty to comply with it. But you will have time to ensure your business is compliant. The time available to implement changes varies by requirement and size of business. We have set out these implementation timings with the description of each remedy.

During this period, we will also engage with the RCVS to formalise its commitment to meet our requirements and make these legally binding. We call this an Undertaking.

### Funding Order

To fund its new role, the RCVS will charge a levy to veterinary businesses. The levy you need to pay is set out in the [Veterinary Services Market Investigation (Funding) Order 2026](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/veterinary-services-market-investigation-funding-order-2026-and-veterinary-services-market-investigation-royal-college-of-veterinary-surgeons-funding-) and depends on the number of FOPs (including outsourced out-of-hours service providers) you own.

## What happens if a veterinary business does not comply with the Order?

If a veterinary business does not comply with its obligations, the CMA could:

- work with a business to change its practices to stop the breach

- issue a binding set of instructions (‘directions’) requiring the business to take steps to comply with the Order

- impose a financial penalty on the business for breaching the Order

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) published its [Final Report](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/veterinary-services-for-household-pets-final-decision-report) on 24 March 2026, concluding its [market investigation into veterinary services for household pets](https://www.gov.uk/cma-cases/veterinary-services-market-for-pets-review) in the UK - **“** _**the most extensive review of veterinary services in the UK in generations**_” in the CMA’s own words. For vets and vet businesses this will be welcomed certainty, and an end to the regulatory scrutiny that has weighed on the industry since the sector first came under review in 2023. As _veterans_ of the industry will remember, this market investigation attracted unprecedented attention, receiving 56,000 responses to the CMA’s Call for Information, and over 450 responses from stakeholders on its consultation on the Provisional Decision.

The Final Report follows the CMA's [Provisional Decision](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/69020040bdb1ef2270a1d0e6/Summary_of_provisional_decision_29_October_1.pdf) published in October 2025 which we reported on [here](https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2025/uk/no-more-paws-for-concern-cmas-provisional-decision-prescribes-major-reforms-for-uk-veterinary-sector). While continuing the direction of travel laid out in the Provisional Decision, the Final Report reflects some important differences with regards to (i) fee caps and (ii) the remedy on written prescriptions that we will cover in this article.

The CMA's Final Report confirms the same three overarching themes identified in the Provisional Decision that we reported on in October 2025 (see link above):

- **Lack of information:** The CMA considers that vets and veterinary businesses are not providing pet owners the information they need to make choices between different practices, treatment options and alternative medicine retailers such as online pharmacies.
- **Barriers to action:** Pet owners face obstacles including uncertainty about online pharmacy quality and timeliness, high prescription fees, delays in obtaining written prescriptions, difficulties making complaints, and barriers preventing First Opinion Practices (FOPs) from switching Out of Hours (OOH) providers.
- **Outdated regulation: In the CMA’s view,**the regulatory regime is " _outdated and wholly unfit for purpose_", particularly because legislation currently applies only to veterinary professionals rather than the businesses employing them.

The CMA cites as its primary concern that average prices of vet services rose by 63% between 2016 and 2023, while acknowledging that vets ultimately work in a commercial industry with businesses needing to make “ _a reasonable profit to continue to provide good quality care and invest in the latest treatments_”. The CMA also welcomes the recent [government consultation on a new Veterinary Surgeons Act](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/reform-of-the-veterinary-surgeons-act-1966), a positive step in addressing the CMA’s recommendation for legislative reform particularly to bring veterinary businesses, rather than just individuals, in scope.

In that context, the CMA has confirmed a wide-ranging package of remedies designed to reset the relationship between veterinary businesses and pet owners which vet businesses will need to consider carefully. Narrowing down the 21 recommendations in the Provisional Decision, the CMA has decided on **14 remedies** that it plans to implement through a CMA Order and Undertakings made to the CMA by the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons (RCVS). These remedies can be grouped into the following 6 categories:

1. **Providing general information on ownership, prices and services;**
2. **Providing information and policies on treatments;**
3. **Prescribing veterinary medicines;**
4. **Managing out-of-hours contracts;**
5. **Offering cremation services; and**
6. **Managing complaints.**

While the changes are due to be implemented in stages (and the CMA’s statutory deadline for putting in place Orders is 23 September 2026), **early preparation for businesses is key**. We [previously set out](https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2025/uk/no-more-paws-for-concern-cmas-provisional-decision-prescribes-major-reforms-for-uk-veterinary-sector) the key areas of preparation businesses should consider:

# Veterinary Client Mediation Service Releases 2023-24 Insight Report

The Veterinary Client Mediation Service has published the annual report of activity and insight from 2024. Funded by the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons and free at the point of service for consumers, the VCMS is an independent and voluntary alternative dispute resolution service. In 2023-24, it received 3,548 enquiries, with 98% within its remit to provide advice and support. The number of enquiries was down -2.6% on the previous 12-month period.

Standards of care are still the main cause of pet owner complaints, according to the latest annual Insight Report for 2023-24, published by The Veterinary Client Mediation Service (VCMS).

Enquiries relating to standard of care were the number one concern for pet owners, accounting for 60% of all complaints, up +4% on the previous year. Within the standards of care category, there was an increase in disputes around unexpected outcomes (+37%) and vets not adequately investigating an issue (+12%), however there was a sharp decrease in misdiagnosis complaints (-30%).

Customer service accounted for 19% of overall complaints, with service and communication around consent increasing the most (+31%). After increasing last year due to the cost-of-living crisis, complaints about clinical fees accounted for just 14% of enquiries in 2023-24, up just +3% year on year. Complaints regarding excessive fees fell -21%, while the most common fee-related issues were around clarity, being kept up to date on charges and cost-benefit analysis on different treatment options.

Overall, the VCMS was able to support more than half (56%) of the enquirers’ to raise and resolve their issues at a local level, with the practice. For those that couldn’t be resolved within the practice’s complaints procedures, the VCMS invited 1,050 veterinary practices to join the mediation process, of which 77% practices accepted. This signifies a +5% improvement on the previous year’s engagement rate. Of the 767 mediated cases in 2023-24 – the highest number of mediations handled in the past 3 years – VCMS was able to achieve an impressive 82% resolution rate.

Through the mediation process, animal owners and practices have been able to agree resolutions to complaints and disputes, and analysis shows that resolutions continued to be a mixture of financial and non-financial outcomes. Resolutions such as apologies, explanations, further treatment or support accounted for 47%, up +4% year on year. In appropriate circumstances, outcomes also included addressing disproportionate or unfair online comments and supporting the future relationship between animal owners and veterinary professionals. Financial resolutions include goodwill gestures (12%), which averaged £420.85, or discounts on fees (13%) as a resolution to the complaint. The VCMS process also helped resolve situations where animal owners had withheld payment of fees. 28% of resolutions involved the issues raised being addressed and the animal owner then settling the outstanding fees. This avoided an escalation to worrying and costly debt recovery processes in these disputes.

Set up in 2017 to support the relationship between vet practices and animal owners, the VCMS has the seal of approval of both sides, with aftercare surveys revealing that 98% of veterinary practices and 96% of clients would use the VCMS again, demonstrating the high levels of satisfaction achieved.

Jennie Jones, Head of the VCMS, commented: _“The issue of complaints and how these are handled within_ _the veterinary sector have been increasingly in the media in recent years, but what our latest report_ _shows in black and white is that when complaints arise, we have the mechanisms in place to resolve them_ _– and to do it quickly and fairly. I’m encouraged to see more practices engaging in mediation this year,_ _especially as almost all would use the service again. That’s testament to the power of having a team of_ _expert of resolution managers on hand to bring even the most emotional and contentious of matters to_ _a satisfactory close for all. Analysis shows that veterinary complaints are complex and not solely linked to_ _costs, with nearly half of resolutions involving communication, explanations and a shared understanding_ _of the situation. We continue to feedback our insight to the veterinary sector to help continuous_ _improvement around communication and supporting positive relationships between animal owners and_ _veterinary practice teams”._

The VCMS continues to advocate for collaborative decision-making and transparent communication, ensuring both veterinary professionals and animal owners are informed and engaged in the care process. The detailed insights and data presented in the latest annual report aim to support ongoing quality improvement within the veterinary community and establish even higher levels of satisfaction among pet owners.
